crime.value: Murder of Father Jim, a Maryknoll priest, by Guatemalan military personnel; central question: what happened to Ryan (journalist) after Jim's death and who was responsible
crime.quote: It was awful to leave Jim's body in the square. But what could he do? Drag the body out of town?

victim.value: Father Jim, a Maryknoll missionary priest working with the poor in Guatemala during civil war; killable because he was American, a priest, and implicitly supporting leftist humanitarian causes
victim.quote: Jim was a Maryknoll, which meant he was dispensing medicine, teaching literacy skills to the poor...encouraging dangerously leftist ideas.

closed_world.value: Small town of Huehuetenango in the Guatemalan highlands during active civil war; bounded by military checkpoints, remote jungle terrain, and political violence with no functional law enforcement
closed_world.quote: There were rumors of recent massacres in the mountains just outside Huehuetenango. Whole villages dumped in the woods.

culprit_and_motive.value: Guatemalan military or paramilitary forces; motive is silencing perceived communist sympathizers and eliminating American witnesses to atrocities during civil war
culprit_and_motive.quote: The military blamed the EGP; the Catholic clergy blamed the military; the military blamed the clergy for supporting the EGP

investigator.value: Ryan's unnamed younger brother, years later, traveling to Guatemala to understand what happened to Ryan and to himself; investigating through memory, interviews, and retracing Ryan's final journey
investigator.quote: Ultimately, I went to Guatemala with two hopes: perhaps I could find out who I was...and maybe my trip could bring a kind of solace to my mother.

suspect_architecture.value: No classical suspect pool. Perpetrators are unnamed young soldiers (ages 16-18) acting under implied military command structure; individual culpability is diffuse and institutional. The military blames rebel group EGP; clergy blame the military — mutual accusation replaces differentiated suspects.
suspect_architecture.quote: The military blamed the EGP; the Catholic clergy blamed the military; the military blamed the clergy for supporting the EGP

red_herring.value: The military's narrative that massacres and killings (including Jim's) were the work of communist rebels (EGP) functions as deliberate institutional misdirection, deflecting accountability from state actors onto guerrillas.
red_herring.quote: Maybe the men who'd done this had moved on, had frightened themselves with killing a gringo, a priest no less. Maybe they'd already been reprimanded

clue_fairness.value: The story is not a fair-play mystery; clues are withheld by design. The narrator-brother explicitly cannot access embassy records, Ryan's final movements are speculative, and the reader is told 'there is no way of knowing' what happened — opacity is thematic, not a puzzle to solve.
clue_fairness.quote: There is no way of knowing if it was the same restaurant, if he'd even gone out to eat at all.

social_world.value: Guatemalan civil-war power structure: military/paramilitary authority over civilian and clerical life; U.S. journalistic/diplomatic class unable or unwilling to intervene; Maryknoll missionaries occupying a dangerous middle position between state and poor; American tourists insulated by privilege and wilful ignorance.
social_world.quote: The political naïveté of the Catholic project in Guatemala was the seed of Ryan's projected article. Though he sympathised with the ideals, it was suicidal.

alibi.value: No alibi structure in the classical sense. The soldiers offer a false pretext ('questions only') as a functional alibi for the abduction, masking lethal intent behind bureaucratic politeness. The U.S. Embassy later offers institutional non-knowledge as its alibi for inaction.
alibi.quote: "Please come out. Questions only," the acned kid says, smiling.

reveal_mechanic.value: There is no reveal. The story's architecture resists resolution: the narrator's investigative trip to Guatemala yields nothing, the embassy shows nothing, and Ryan's fate is rendered through free-indirect speculation rather than evidence. Absence of revelation is itself the structural statement.
reveal_mechanic.quote: What I found during those six weeks in Central America wasn't what I'd been looking for. Nothing had been resolved.

media_and_audience.value: Ryan's journalist career frames the crime's media dimension: he believes a survivor's eyewitness account could force American newspapers to care about Guatemalan massacres, yet his own disappearance will go unrecorded. The world's indifference to atrocity — 'the world just didn't care' — is both theme and structural irony.
media_and_audience.quote: If Jim could hook him up with this woman not even American newspapers would be able to ignore the article. Ryan could, with some luck, make the world care.

investigator_wound.value: The narrator-brother's wound is identity deficit and survivor's guilt: he feels his 'self was in some ways missing' and attributes this to Ryan's disappearance. His investigation is driven not by professional duty but by a need to forge selfhood through action — making him emotionally unreliable and his search structurally doomed.
investigator_wound.quote: Perhaps I could find out who I was — I'd always felt my self was in some ways missing and was connected to the mystery of what had happened to Ryan
